source_read: PDF (journal download of an old scan), pp. 955-961, all 7 pages read on pages rendered at 150 dpi (the text layer is incomplete: Table 1's 'Since' column and Table 2 are garbled in it). Tables 1-3 read on the rendered pages; the Figure (p. 956), including the inset, read at 300 dpi against the 10-point gridlines (values approximate to 1-2 points). No supplement; the 1974 monograph (ref. 1) not read.

claims.overstatement: One part is not accurate as worded: 'whether any had treatment is not reported' (and the closing 'for the Vietnam veterans, treatment was not reported'). The paper says the departure urine screening that began in June 1971 was meant to identify and detain men with positive urine for detoxification and treatment (p. 955), that the one-month cohort was chosen so the men had similar opportunities for treatment in the military (p. 956), and Table 3 reports psychiatric treatment since return (for example 12% of the 33 general-sample men who used narcotics in Vietnam and no drugs after return; p. 960). What the paper does not report is how many men received drug treatment, before or after return, or how treatment related to remission. Suggested wording: 'how many had treatment for drug use is not reported (men with a positive urine test at departure were to be held for detoxification and treatment)'. The claim does not call the remission untreated, which is correct.
claims.note: Every Robins number in the statement and magnitude was found on the rendered pages: 470 general sample and September 1971 (p. 956); 451 interviewed (p. 957; Table 1 footnote, p. 959); interviews 8-12 months after return (p. 956); narcotics 11/43/10%, self-reported addiction 0.2/20/0.7%, study criteria 0.4/21/1% (Table 1, p. 959); about a third tried heroin (p. 957); 134 still addicted at departure, 50% any narcotic and 14% dependent after return (Table 2, p. 959; text p. 958); 95% remission (p. 958); Figure about 2% of 90 (general) and about 7% of 341 (drug-positive) addicted again (p. 956; my 300-dpi reading 2.1% and 7.1%). Three qualifications, none changing a figure: (1) 'combined without weighting' is an inference from Table 2's Ns summing to 898, the number interviewed in both samples; the table does not name its sample(s). (2) The Results open by saying results are for the general sample unless otherwise noted (p. 956), so by the paper's own convention the 95% would be a general-sample figure, yet the Figure's general-sample value implies about 98% remission and Table 2's 426 previously addicted men about 92% (my calculation, about 8% dependent); the 95% cannot be reproduced, and 'without saying which sample it describes' is a fair summary. (3) The drug-positive sample is defined in the Methods by a positive departure urine test for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (p. 956), as the claim says; the abstract says opiates (p. 955). The paper's term is 'addiction'; Table 1 labels the study's criteria 'symptoms of dependence', so 'dependent ... by the study's own criteria' is fair. Not in the claim but relevant to 'remission': heavy use, injection and heroin preference after return exceeded pre-service levels (p. 959), and new cases kept emerging through the post-return period (p. 961).

anchors.extracted: About 13,760 Army enlisted men and draftees returned from Vietnam to the US in September 1971; a random 'general sample' of 470 was drawn from Department of Defense lists; of the returnees about 1,400 had a departure urine test positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates, from whom a random 'drug-positive sample' of 495 was drawn; 22 men were in both (943 in all). The abstract (p. 955) describes the drug-positive sample as positive for opiates.

Men were sought for interview between May and September 1972, 8 to 12 months after return; of the 943, 95% were interviewed, 92% gave urine and military records were obtained for 99%; 97% of men whose records showed heroin use in Vietnam reported it at interview.

anchors.locator: Results > Drug Use in Vietnam, tabulation and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Interviewed general sample N = 451: 43% used a narcotic at least once in Vietnam; about one third tried heroin (and about one third opium). Of the 196 who tried narcotics, 46% reported addiction and 47% met the study's criteria; for the whole general sample, 20% reported addiction in Vietnam and 21% met the criteria (three of four: more-than-weekly use for over a month; at least two of chills, stomach cramps, insomnia, muscle pain on withdrawal; withdrawal lasting 2 days, or 12 hours if modified; believing oneself addicted).
Before Vietnam / in Vietnam / since return: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; addiction by self-report 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%; addiction by the study's criteria ('symptoms of dependence') 0.4% / 21% / 1%.

anchors.locator: Results > Drug Use After Vietnam, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: About half of the men who used narcotics in Vietnam had become addicted, against 7% of men who used narcotics after return; the authors state addiction remission rates of 95% for men addicted in Vietnam, with no sample or denominator, and set them beside young patients treated at the Lexington and Fort Worth federal hospitals re-examined six months later. The Results open (p. 956, 1st paragraph) by saying figures are for the general sample unless otherwise noted.

anchors.locator: Figure (narcotic use 8 to 10 months after Vietnam by men first addicted in Vietnam)
anchors.extracted: Read approximately at 300 dpi: general sample (N = 90) about 65% no use, 21-22% light use, 12% heavy use, 2% addiction; drug-positive sample (N = 341) about 61%, 21-22%, 10%, 7%; 122 NARA patients six months after release to aftercare about 11%, 6%, 14%, 70%. About a third of the men first addicted in Vietnam used narcotics again without being addicted. Light and heavy use are not defined.

anchors.locator: Table 2; Results > Drug Use After Vietnam, 2nd paragraph (p. 958)
anchors.extracted: Men still addicted at departure who said they were detected because too addicted to stop (n = 134): 50% used any narcotic and 14% were dependent after return (text: half stopped entirely); previously addicted and still using at departure (155): 35% and 5%; previously addicted, no use in last 3 days (137): 33% and 5%. Row Ns sum to 898, the number interviewed in both samples; neither sample nor weighting is stated. Men had been back about ten months on average; resumption mostly began within four months.

From June 1971 men due to leave Vietnam had mandatory urine screening intended to identify and detain those with recent illicit drug use for detoxification and treatment; the September 1971 cohort was chosen so the men had similar exposure to drugs, similar opportunities for treatment in the military and the same time after return. Drug treatment actually received is not reported.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (general-sample men who used narcotics in Vietnam, N = 196)
anchors.extracted: Psychiatric treatment since return by drug used after return: narcotics (n = 43) 26%, amphetamine or barbiturate (49) 12%, marijuana only (71) 6%, none (33) 12%; the kind of treatment is not specified.

anchors.locator: Results > Drug Use After Vietnam, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Heavy use did not fall back to pre-service levels: since return 3% had a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use (under 0.5% before); injection became the preferred route of 63% of frequent narcotic users and heroin replaced codeine as the narcotic most used.

The authors say it remains a question whether the background characteristics that distinguish the returnees from typical US patients, or the change in the social context of use between Vietnam and the US, explains the high remission rates.

Limits stated: the short tour may account for the remission; concealment possible though judged unlikely; Vietnam atypical and the sample homogeneous in age, sex, occupation and period, so findings may not apply elsewhere; new cases emerged throughout the post-return period, so the long-term outcome is unknown (a three-year follow-up with a matched nonveteran group was under way).

key_findings.correction: My 300-dpi reading agrees within 1 point: general about 65/21-22/12/2, drug-positive about 61/21-22/10/7, NARA about 11/6/14/70; the two light-use markers overlap at 21-22% and cannot be told apart. Inset about 44/33/10/12; its triangle markers are the drug-positive sample's symbol in the main legend, although the inset's sample is not stated.

reporting_issues.note: Add: the Results open by saying figures are for the general sample unless otherwise noted (p. 956, Results, 1st paragraph), so by the paper's own convention the 95% would be a general-sample figure, which the Figure (about 2% addicted again, about 98% remission) does not match. Recomputed Table 2: 33.4 of 426 dependent (7.8%).
Daggers mark drug-related problem, arrest, psychiatric treatment and unemployment; the double dagger (drug users above nonusers) marks divorce only.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI moderate is reasonable: random, nearly complete samples with blind interviewers, against self-reported and partly retrospective use, non-standard criteria, an unreported urine check after return and a short window. Recomputed Wilson intervals match the card within 0.2 points.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The abstract's 'essentially decreased to pre-Vietnam levels' against the rise in heavy use and injection (p. 959), and the causal turn on p. 960, are both on the pages cited.

missed: Treatment is reported in part, contrary to cannot_establish and the risk-of-bias reasoning ('treatment before or after return is not reported'): the departure urine screening was meant to detain men with positive urine for detoxification and treatment (p. 955, Introduction, 1st paragraph); the cohort was chosen for similar opportunities for treatment in the military (p. 955, Methods, 1st paragraph, continuing p. 956); Table 3 reports psychiatric treatment since return (26/12/6/12%, p. 960). What is not reported is drug treatment received per man or its relation to remission. The card should say that, and that the 134 men detected at departure 'because too addicted to quit' were the program's target.
The Results' convention that figures are for the general sample unless otherwise noted (p. 956, Results, 1st paragraph) bears on reporting issue 1 (the 95%).
Locator detail: the Methods' 1st paragraph (September 1971 chosen; similar treatment opportunities) starts on p. 955 and continues on p. 956; the card's recruitment field cites it as p. 956.
